newsitem.title: UK: Investors "unsettled" at new DMG fund saga.
newsitem.headline: Investors "unsettled" at new DMG fund saga.

text.p: Pension fund clients are unsettled by the latest row at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell over the suspension of top fund manager Nicola Horlick and will be assessing whether to move their business, industry sources said.
"Clients are definitely worried. They look for continuity, stability," John Conroy, European head of asset consulting at pension fund consultant Towers Perrin, told Reuters on Thursday.
"It is very important there is some sense of how a place (investment house) is organised and resourced...that what I am told today holds for some time in the future."
"But bear in mind all we have at the moment is a series of allegations," he added.

Horlick, head of Morgan Grenfell Asset Managment's (MGAM) 18 billion sterling pension fund business, was suspended on Tuesday for "possible breach of contract" after she was allegedly discovered planning to jump ship and take some of her 30-strong team and clients with her.
Banking sources said Morgan Grenfell had been holding talks to reassure major clients that business was continuing as usual, despite Horlick's suspension.

David Adam, chief executive officer of the Railway Pension Trustee Company, which has 1.25 billion sterling with MGAM, confirmed he had met company officials. "Yes, they came round to see me at their request to explain what had happened. We keep close to all of our asset managers because we are a large scheme but we will be keeping even closer than we would have in the coming months." "We have very large amounts of money which we are custodians for but we need to be sure that we are as least as confident of the firm we are transferring to as the one we are tranferring from." He added it was "unfortunate" that some consultants appeared to "give an immediate knee jerk reaction" to the situation.
There was some speculation key clients could switch fund managers even though they had stuck with MGAM through the sacking last year of another high-profile fund manager, Peter Young.
"MGAM clients are very keen to find out what is happening and they will be very upset by this latest saga," said one consultant, who declined to be named.

"When we prepare beauty lists' of possible managers for clients, we show the results but also have to demonstrate we understand the investment process and the personal contribution of the people involved. Clients are naturally going to be concerned if someone who is driving the process is faltering."

Consultants noted that Horlick was part of the top rank MGAM team which reassured institutional investors after the Young affair. "Yes, she was involved in the hand holding, so that does make clients nervous," said Tower Perrin's Conroy.
Deutsche has said they do not expect an exodus of pension fund clients because they "understand that their business is managed by a team and not just an individual".
"The feedback was that they are not going to make any hasty decisions," said spokesman James Murray.

Other industry sources agree pension fund trustees are naturally conservative and would not switch managers on a whim or a rumour. But with annual mandate reviews coming up, the storm could not have blown up at a worse time for MGAM. There are queries about exactly why Horlick, who was perceived to be in line to replace Keith Percy, the chief investment officer axed after the Young affair, might have wished to leave.
"She was with a successful, solid gold house and they seemed to be hanging onto clients after their last crisis. Why was she straying ?," asked one funds industry source.
Fund managers said there were suggestions that Horlick might leave MGAM in the wake of the furore and that others could follow.
Conroy reflected similar concern, "If a number of managers are going to leave, that is a serious issue, it affects the credibility of the organisation going forward."
